utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam and Mr. Oric can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good afternoon to you, too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours and also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, within my team also including Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and I appear here today with co-counsel, Mr. John Jones, and Ms. Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good afternoon to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour which concerns the exhibit list filed by the Prosecution for this witness, for today's witness, and it's to anticipate an objection which I'll have. If, firstly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to put you -- I haven't seen the list. I'm not even aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. There is -- it's dated -- well, we received one and there are seven items on it, eight items and it's dated 24 January 2006 and, as I understand it, two of those exhibits are reports by the Prosecution's experts and I would simply say this: That we didn't ask Professor Bilic to analyse the reports of the Prosecution experts and we don't think it's appropriate for him to be asked to comment on their reports. It wasn't part of his mission. It wasn't part of his mandate. He's here to present his opinion. They presented their opinion. And we would certainly object to him being asked to comment on their reports, particularly when he hasn't analysed it, or be asked to conduct some ad hoc analysis. And secondly, on the list there are other documents which have not been analysed by Professor Bilic in his report, and it's somewhat ironic that the Prosecution are proposing to show new documents to this witness which he didn't analyse, given that Mr. Wubben objected to any notion that I would show new documents to the witness. In the event the documents I showed were purely and simply to show a water-mark which is something which anyone could see. It wasn't a question of analysis. It was a question of visual demonstration, and again I would submit it's not appropriate to ask this expert to conduct an ad hoc analysis of a signature on a document which he hasn't analysed. I anticipate that in any event, the expert will give an answer to that effect but I simply want to signal beforehand that that will be my objection so that we don't necessarily have to have the witness out when that matter arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, of course, Mr. Jones do you wish to answer to the points raised by Mr. Jones, Mr. Wubben, before I speak my own mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, let me first find out how this technical will be developed to put on and off the microphone and at the same time can anyone hear me. Well, first, the reports by the Prosecution experts were not enlisted to -- with the aim to comment by the expert. They were enlisted that whenever I refer or the Judges will ask questions about the report, referring to it, then that we have available such an exhibit, and about the other documents, these are not new documents, these are known -- these are already tendered documents confirmed as the so-called known signatures, known signatures from K9 up to K35. And these should be available as I want to demonstrate also on -- in the same way as Mr. Jones has done, with previous new documents, to demonstrate what is possible to be seen without a expert examination for everybody, and to ask his opinion about that. So not an expertise comment but the same as envisaged by Mr. Jones when he introduced new documents, his opinion standing this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both, Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben. I think we would rather reserve our position as we go along because obviously I haven't seen these documents. Today I don't even know what documents he's referring to. And as we go along we see what the question is, just as was the case yesterday with the documents with the finger -- with the water-mark. At the time I was very much taken by surprise by the position taken by the Prosecution because I simply couldn't understand it, but we'll see, we'll play it by the ear as we go along, of course. And as far as certain preoccupations are concerned that you expressed, I'm sure that the expert witness will know how to handle that, Mr. Jones. Yes. There are a few things I would like to mention. We will be working hard this weekend, all of us, trying to divide our work, particularly because there is a lot to read. There are the following motions: One dealing with the request of the Defence for the -- in relation to the interview with the so-called interview with the Accused. The other one with regard to Exhibit P84. And then this last motion on rebuttal, which is accompanied -- has about two inches' thickness of attachment to it. We need to know beforehand, we were discussing this in my room from -- practically from 1.00 until now, and other matters. We need to know exactly where you stand time wise for example with regard to the two motions filed by the Defence, where do you stand, Mr. Wubben? When are we to expect your responses, without necessitating on our part having to clamp down and fix shorter limit than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We cannot state for sure. We are at the stage of organising the relevant information to -- for example, with translation, to enable CLSS to work on it and to find out what is the background and also the legal consequences, specific related to that other motion of the interview of the Accused, and Your Honours, please, be assured that we are working at a fast speed on it and now at the very moment and already yesterday started, altogether. So I cannot envisage because these are voluminous motions, I can't give you a specific date but perhaps in the beginning of the following week, I think I can give you more specific terms in -- as it comes to the time needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are no where near as voluminous as yours basically. I mean, there isn't much. It's a question of the translation process that you have been given pretty much advance notice of and that we have understood throughout that you were -- you had undertaken this exercise with regard to P84 and also the interview a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but this is a pleading not only for translation but with a view to the interview forming a basis for excluding it with very legal propositions. So we had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is nothing voluminous there. That's a simple argument. What we need to know very quickly, if this is possible, is this: That in relation to the interview, for example, the Defence has taken the trouble to separate the transcript into two parts, your transcript and what they submit should be the correct transcript. And there are various instances, I mean, detailed. If you are in a position, which I think you should be now, to accept that the transcript should be like or as submitted by the Defence, then please tell us. At least you tell us that. It would spare us having to go through a lot of exercise ourselves. That's number one. In other words, this exercise, I think, should have been carried -- I mean, of course, you did not have specific reference to specific parts but now you do. And I haven't gone through the totality of those excerpts but if you are in a position -- I meant to do that yesterday but I wasn't feeling well at all and I ended up not doing it but if you are in a position to at least conclude that, then obviously the -- what will remain is submissions on the rest, which form the basis of the Defence request for the removal from the evidence of the -- expunging of the evidence of the statement of the -- or the interview of the Accused. P84, again, I mean, P84 has been the point of reference during the proceedings from both Prosecution and Defence, and the contestation throughout has been mostly in relation to the interpretation, the translation. So if it is ready, we can't delay the case depending and waiting for CLSS to finalise a translation. I'm making this very clear. If there has been an allegation that the translation is defective or leaves much to be desired, then that should have been attended to. I turn to you now, Madam Vidovic and Mr. Jones in relation to the rebuttal. And I am drawing your attention to this because you had anticipated without even knowing who was going to be named for purposes of rebuttal, you had anticipated an objection. So if you still are of the same opinion, please come forward as soon as you can. Now you have got all the details, or relatively speak speaking all the details. Perhaps you can let us know, not necessarily now, when we'll have the pleasure of having a response from you because obviously the outcome of the issue between you depends -- we'll need first to reach our decision and if there is going to be a rebuttal, there needs to be sufficient time to allow the Prosecution to bring over their witness, if that's the case. And then, of course, please do start thinking about possible rejoinder. I think from your experience you should be more or less in a position to know where you stand when it comes to the rebuttal and therefore whether there will be a case for rejoinder or not. But I think please do come back to us as early as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I might just say this. At present, Your Honour, because it does impact on the schedule of the coming weeks obviously, that indeed as Your Honour has observed this is voluminous, I have it here, it's several inches thick. Granted the motion is eight pages and the rest are attachments but nonetheless we have to review all of it. But it's true we certainly -- having reviewed it, we certainly will oppose these witnesses being called in rebuttal because we say that they are not true rebuttal witnesses at all. In fact, they are people about whom the Prosecution knew during the Prosecution case, they decided for, I say, for tactical reasons, I don't mean that in a pejorative way, but they decided for tactical reasons not to call those people at the time and that it would be inappropriate for plainly wrong to call these witnesses after our case to have a second bite at the cherry. So we intend to vigorously oppose this, for us it's a very important point of principle that the Prosecution not to be allowed to call evidence going to issues which have always been issues in this trial, going to command and control or organisation or disorganisation of any armed forces. And so we need to first of all address the arguments by the Prosecution as to why they say this is actually rebuttal evidence. We need to counter that by pointing to the pre-trial brief the opening speech, our cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, to say that all these issues were live while the Prosecution still had a chance to call these witnesses. And that involves a lot of reviewing of the transcripts, the pre-trial briefs, et cetera. And so certainly we do intend to file a vigorous response opposing, vigorous opposition. And I might say that also, given the importance of this, if Your Honours are against us we will seek leave to appeal naturally because it does have profound implications for us, and I think that does need to be built into the schedule obviously, in that what we wouldn't want to be is overtaken by events so that a schedule which is put together in the interests of -- legitimate interests of efficiency that a Prosecution rebuttal be scheduled to start next week or the week after, so that in fact there isn't sufficient time either for us to file a response or for Your Honours to consider the matter or for leave to appeal to be sought. And so I think to be realistic it would be almost impossible to envisage a rebuttal case starting in the next couple of weeks simply because all these steps have to be gone through. But I simply make those remarks. It's a matter for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously but whether you -- the only thing you haven't told us is when to expect your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, for the moment we would say we need the full period allowed under Rule 126 bis which would be 14 days, and if Your Honours wish to impose a shorter time limit then we'll obviously abide by it. But we -- for the record that's what we say we need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We haven't discussed this, Judge Eser, Judge Brydensholt and myself. We'll discuss it and we'll tell you tomorrow; both of you, actually, now that we have heard what your submissions are. We could also decide during the break actually but the other thing is this, that Professor Bilic has finished his testimony in chief, and the position as it emerges is that some of the documents that were not in evidence before have been tendered in evidence in a way that they have been tendered. There are several other documents that Professor Bilic has himself stated he has made use of, which I understand were handed to him by your team, which are not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The N documents the contentious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example the specimens of handwriting or signatures by Sacirovic, Fejzic, this is what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I need to draw this argument much further but if they are not available to our expert, there is no point in asking him to examine the same document that were examined by your -- so although we are not of course in a position as I explained earlier we cannot tell you, you have to file these documents. There is more than one reason for that. At the same time we are being very frank with you, what the position is, that if there is nothing for the expert to make a comparison with, he's going to tell us. So think about it a little bit, the decision, of course, will ultimately remain yours and not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We can probably revert to you on that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm mentioning it because I keep conducting this trial in as constructive manner as possible. So that being so, I think we can bring in the witness. I see you -- is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request that Mr. Gramsci di Fazio to make a short submission regarding the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. MR. DI FAZIO: Just this, Your Honours. One would have expected known signatures that an expert is providing provides one of the fundamental bases of his report, one of the three main areas of evidence, and he's analysing known -- contentious signatures of Hamdija Fejzic and is using known signatures. It's a fundamental basis for his expert opinion about those contentious signatures. Those signatures, known signatures, have not been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And should have been done so through the expert. I mean one would think as I understand the situation, I don't know if there is going to be evidence about this but as I understand the situation, he provided, Fejzic provided the signatures to this expert. We've never seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: That's a problem for the Defence, isn't it? And the Prosecution would object to any recalling of Bilic to examine him in chief and reintroduce the documents. It's a matter that the Defence should have attended to and should have, and it stands out, it stands out clearly, it's a fundamental thing, fundamental matter, that they should have provided those documents. The consequences that Your Honour has just adverted to flow from their mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond to that? It's certainly not a mistake. We haven't made any mistakes whatsoever. The Prosecution are forgetting two things. Firstly they never asked for these non-contentious signatures, which is actually quite extraordinary if one wants to talk about mistakes and extraordinary behaviour. Prosecution has never written to us to request or to be provided with those documents, and it might be an oversight by them. I don't think it's helpful for either of us -- either side to be casting aspersions or criticism at the other side or to say what the necessary consequences will be of a particular course of action. The fact is, the Prosecution - it's the second matter I think they have forgotten - is they have the burden of proving the authenticity of documents which they tender in evidence, and if we call evidence to the effect that some of those documents are not authentic we will do that and we will do that in a way we see fit. And it will be a matter for Your Honours to weigh -- to decide what weight to give to that evidence. And it's certainly not a rule of law that, unless we provide a certain document, then Professor Bilic's testimony evaporates as being irrelevant. It's still a matter of what weight you give to it. And I might just say that obviously one of the categories of non-contentious signatures is that of our client as well, and Your Honour fully appreciates the issues of disclosing non-contentious signatures of our client. In those circumstances, there is a real question about whether if we are not going to disclose those, whether it makes sense to disclose the others of Hamdija Fejzic and Hamed Salihovic. In any event I said we would revert after the break as to whether we intend to offer those but if we don't it's not shocking, it's not unexpected. It's whatever Your Honours decide to make of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's definitely not shocking, and in fact, anyone who has worked as a Defence counsel would know exactly why you have done it. Have you ever worked as a Defence counsel, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honours, for 13 years in Australia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you know exactly what's cooking at the moment and that's why we haven't intervened because although we can leave matters to stand as we are, with you carrying the burden of proof and they carrying no burden and being sufficiently happy enough to throw in that reasonable doubt, we still believe we should be in a position whereby we can try to find out the truth. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that, Your Honours. No, I understand it, Your Honours. And, of course, the procedures that might be adopted in the situation in common law jurisdictions don't of necessity apply here. I understand that. I understand that. But the point is that I wanted to make is that it's not for the Prosecution to call upon the Defence to ask for documents that should have been included in the report. I just make that point. It's not for us to present their case. In other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The point, Mr. Di Fazio, is you're jumping to the conclusion that they should have been included in the report. Well, let's say it would have been much better if they were included in the report, and that would have been the normal thing to do. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not including them in the report is also a possibility which is acknowledged. Which is acknowledged. So at this point in time we'll deal with it later on depending on what the decision will be. Let's leave it here and we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while the witness is being brought it I should pledges that we are filing a motion today. I can assure you it's not a lengthy motion. It's two pages, I believe, and it's a request for an order that we be permitted to inspect certain material. And I just mention that. We can provide a courtesy copy during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To inspect what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To inspect certain material in the possession of the Prosecution. It will be -- it's very self explanatory, but I mention that just since we were reviewing the motions which have been filed, and it may be in light of the discussion just now that we'll file a motion regarding signatures in possession of the Prosecution, of Hamed Salihovic, but that's a matter that I'll deal with in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have no comment on that other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't want to answer his motion before you see it, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No but there is, of course, 66(B). Apart from that, Your Honours, we will file as well a motion today in response to the request by the Defence counsel in the Srebrenica case to get access to information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't get this. In the Srebrenica case, in the mega-trial, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. There is a request to get access to Oric case files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The Miletic motion or something like that. Miletic, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I was expecting a response from you. You are going to response to it or are you going to file it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all right. Thank you. I have got already someone working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Professor, good afternoon to you and my apologies to you for having kept you waiting but we are always kept busy by the lawyers in this case so we had some procedural matters to talk about and discuss. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to be cross-examined by Mr. Wubben who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Wubben:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Bilic.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have questions for you and I invite to you limit yourself to a short answer if possible, that means a yes or no or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, the break will be at 4.00. So you have an hour and 12 -- and 10 minutes. We'll have one break today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your CV, you mention, Professor Bilic, societies of court experts, you're a member of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're at the same time a member of professional handwriting associations?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except for handwriting, these are associations, not just handwriting, that's to say. These are associations embracing experts of all different fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are on a national level?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, these are associations at the federal level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is the Federal Association of Expert Witnesses. And there is the Association of Expert Witnesses of Republika Srpska, and I'm a member of both associations. That's the situation before the two associations become united and then we will all be together under the one umbrella.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you also a member of an international association?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have occasion to become one. There was a war on and this is something that lies ahead of us, to take that step.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also you didn't try after the war?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am still in the process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned last Monday that in that field you have regular meetings with colleagues to harmonise work and methods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many meetings should I take for that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such meetings. Whenever we have occasion to, we meet, be it in court or in other places, in our offices. These are all junior colleagues of mine. I used to be their mentor, and we still meet quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's in the field of you, Professor, teaching the juniors?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I taught many. Some of them turned out to be very good experts. Others didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also include in those meetings proficiency tests in which you yourself participate?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand tests. For what and who is tested? I don't find this clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We examine different cases together, discuss them, and try to take a common view on matters, consult each other. In fact, we make use of these meetings to see where we stand and whether we share the same language in relation to some cases because there are many cases that are very complex and it's much better for two or three experts to meet together and discuss these things. That would be as much as I have to say on that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, does it mean that on a regular basis, you will not exercise such proficiency tests as being organised as such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you understood the question? Because I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me modify my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, professional associations on the international level enable experts, handwriting experts, to submit themselves to proficiency tests in which afterwards, after the test, results of such test compared with colleagues all over the world, and then it is a kind of outcome from a neutral expert laboratory that you enable yourself to see the outcome of such a test. Are you a member of such an association?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said right at the start that I cannot be a member of an association unless my country is a member, be it in Europe or in the world. Before the war, I lived in such a state system where I could not be a member of an association where the country did not have an agreement to that effect. I worked for state services. However, we do strive towards that now, to become part of the international community and automatically, it will become possible also for us to take part in these matters that you've been mentioning, because the colleagues that I meet with all work for the state institutions and they cannot get involved in these matters without the approval of their employer, their institutions. The proficiency tests you've been mentioning are indeed a positive thing for one's expertise and we will indeed endeavour to become involved in something of the sort, to maintain and improve our expertise. If I've understood you well, I've been testing myself for 30 years now and I do that all the time. That's the sort of job I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, the question was not testing yourself but I can take it that therefore you do not participate in any form of peer review with international colleagues, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had such an opportunity so far, although I would wish to. I've told you the sort of environment I work in, and that's as far as I can answer your question, Your Honour. That's as far as I can go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, in a similar way, do you participate or submit yourself to shared audits for standard operation procedures regarding handwriting examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather prefer, Mr. Wubben, that you explained your question a little bit better. As it is, it may not necessarily elicit the answer that perhaps you have in mind and we want to make sure that both the question -- that the question is properly understood by everyone, in the same manner, so that Professor Bilic is put in a position where he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I will modify my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, there are -- are you aware of international standard operations, procedures?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that it is possible for any company's service to acquire an audit in that respect in order to find out about the level of quality of the standard operation procedure?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you at all. We seem to be running in circles. I simply don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I asked you to put your question in a more -- in more simple terms because to tell him shared audits for standard operation procedures, the system functions differently in different parts of the world and there is -- there is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can't have as a starting point that one section of the world is simply better or if a system is functioning in one place then if it isn't functioning in another place -- then I think -- I know exactly what you mean but I think you ought to put to the witness your question in more clear terms. Otherwise you're not going to have a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- Professor Bilic, did you describe your methods for examination, analysis and findings, did you describe it as the standard operation procedure for yourself, for your institution, for your company?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apply the standard procedure for document examiners. Of course, the equipment may change because every year new equipment is developed, but the procedure of all examiners, be they in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Netherlands or Italy, is the same. It cannot be different. These are part of general knowledge. They cannot be knowledge of only one country or only one part of the world. I hail, of course, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is what we apply there. That's what I can tell you in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, that standard procedure that you use, have you described it in written form?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a concise form. It is part of the written findings I provided, but it was in a very concise form. It could have been expounded it could have taken up as many as 150 pages, it could have been a treatise in fact, in relation to the examination I was required to carry out here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, around 300 pages, that might do an international standard, an international adopted standard. Do you compare that standard you adopted, that written standard --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say 300, I said 150.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. 150 pages. Do you compare that written standard procedure with other procedures from other countries or submit yourself to an international standard organisation?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submit to the international standards and I use the literature that contains these. How else would I be able to do my job? You seem to be angling for the fact that I am a bad expert for the fact that I am not a member of an international association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I would like to make contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not follow you any more. I don't understand you fully. We seem to be revolving around this all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For me, Professor Bilic, let me first state that I have no knowledge about, as an expert, nor as a judge, to give an opinion about your qualities. What I'm here for is to ask you questions that are relevant to elicit in the field of the quality of your work and it is up to the Judges to decide upon it. So that's my responsibility. I don't draw any conclusions. It is just information.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put then my final question in that regard, very simple. So you don't have a description of your operations procedures that you send to an international organisation or a similar association to examine, to compare that description with international accepted standards?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question, please? Can you give me the specific question, laconica brevitas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is do you send your description of the methods, examinations and findings, so the operational procedures, the description, to associations, in order to compare these -- these descriptions with international accepted standards?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this particular case I worked on is concerned, I was clearly told that this was the sort of case that could not be made known to the general public, that the documents I had in my possession --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were confidential documents under the Tribunal, and on the basis of the instructions I was given -- please can I be allowed to finish my question? I could have gone over to see my colleagues in Zagreb or Belgrade even to see a colleague of mine in Banja Luka who is very good at what he does. I could have gone to Skopje in Macedonia and carry out these compare sons. I could not have consulted with my colleagues from the former Yugoslavia -- from outside the former Yugoslavia, because we were dealing with the type of script and the Bosnian language. So I could not have consulted with someone from, let's say, Hungary. I cautioned about that when we were talking about the type of script and the style of writing, et cetera. Generally speaking, of course, I do appreciate the international standards, published world wide, and I do consult these and apply them in my work. So it's not that I am ignorant of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have actually either understood or answered the question. The question was very simple. If someone were to try and establish whether the standards that you use are comparable to accepted international standards, what would he or she have to go by? Is there anything originating from you that would give an idea to others as to what standards you use and how you use those standards? This is basically what you are after, no, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because he hasn't answered that question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He hasn't answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, if I am not who I am but I want to know exactly whether I could trust you with an expert job, the first thing that I would want to know and make sure of is that the standards that you use are accepted, international standards. How would I be able to know that, not knowing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would be able to know that if another expert were hired from the same field of expertise, and then you would be able to satisfy yourself. I think that in this case, the only possible thing would have been to have two experts independently working on this and then comparing their findings. However, I worked on my own, and I didn't have anyone to compare my findings with. I believe I understood your question well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Professor Bilic. Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to make it easier, at the end of your report, you give a list of literature which you seem to have -- which you use when preparing your expertise. Now, does there exist any articles or book of you on your methods which could be included in this list of literature and which may be known to other experts in your field? I think you know your list of literature at the end of your report. Your name is not mentioned there so the question is: Does there exist any publication of you which is somehow subjected to academic peer review?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer your question, Your Honour. In my CV that I handed over here, I put down whatever I published and where it was published. These were articles concerning the identification of electric typewriters, identification of passports in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the identification of bank notes, of money. These are articles that I published. I did not mention them specifically here although I could have. And these articles also contained the methods and principles of my work. I could have well brought them along, these magazines where this was published, the journals, had I known that this would have been raised here. One of them was published by a journal issued at the university of Sarajevo, criminology. One article was commissioned by the central bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then there was another article which was published in Croatia where methods of identification of electronic typewriters were published, which was the first time they were published ever, these particular findings. And there were several other articles in -- that were published. However, I do intend to start writing more than I have so far and perhaps my prospective membership in an international association will also contribute to that. That's my answer to you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I just say I think the witness is having trouble with his headphones. I just wonder if he could be helped so that -- he put them uncomfortably. I've noticed that in the last ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you help the witness a little bit, please? What's the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't seem to make them fit on my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I put them down there, then they keep falling off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you can expand them, extend the length.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it better now? Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will continue. Indeed in your CV, Professor Bilic, you refer to articles you published. How long do you already work as an expert, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Expert in what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Expert in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because he's an expert in other things as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been an expert on documents or for documents. However, within that category, there are very specific fields. For example, expertise on typewriters, on signatures, on stamps, on additions, and so on and so forth. There is no expert anywhere who can say that he is only an expert on signatures. A signature is always attached to a document. So in my view, one is an expert on the scientific study of documents. That's what I have tried to clarify, Your Honours. I have been doing this for 30 years, since 1976. When I graduated from university, I started doing this, and I have been doing only this in the Ministry of the Interior first, then when I left the police, I continued working independently. I have often been called to testify in court. I have been tried and tested in this field, which is probably why the Defence team recruited me. I didn't ask them to recruit me. They must have had their reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, you gave a quite extensive answer. I appreciate it. But the question was only how many years. Your answer is 30 years. Now within those 30 years, is that included 30 years of expertise on signatures?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- you -- sorry. You published three articles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I get the impression that he was going to answer, to give us more information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as an expert, you cannot analyse only a signature. You also have to look at the handwriting, the numbers, the typewriters used or the printers. This is a field where everything is interconnected. You're trying to say that there is a specialty only for signatures. This might be the case in a large institute with many staff members. In my country, I don't have that at my disposal, nor have I had, although I do hope we will have something like that in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's pretty much the same in my country but I think the question that Mr. Wubben or the answer that Mr. Wubben is eliciting from you is the following. Throughout these 30 years of your career as an expert on documents, have you consistently and constantly throughout these 30 years examined also signatures? Or is the examination of signatures only limited to a certain part of those 30 years? This is the question that Mr. Wubben wants to know from you or the information that Mr. Wubben wants to know from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand a little better now and I will respond. I seem to be having difficulty understanding, but I do understand you now, Your Honour, so I will respond. I have constantly worked with signatures and I can say that this is my personal preference. This is what I like doing best. This is a feeling one develops working over time and I have always preferred examining signatures, handwriting. Seals and so on do not present so much of a challenge to me and are not as interesting to me as signatures are. I worked on a court case in Bosnia-Herzegovina involving embezzlement, tax evasion, fraud and so on, involving thousands of signatures and this is what I like doing best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, I take it that you published three articles in 1989, in 1999 and 2002, and you gave information regarding that -- those articles. Did you publish any more articles?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were only of an internal character, within the service I was working for. I wrote instructions which I was unable to publish because they were written for the institution that employed me. I was also engaged on a large-scale research for my M.Sc., which vanished in the war. I analysed the signatures of over 500 students to demonstrate how signatures come into existence, how they are generated, and in 1992, my literature and all my papers were destroyed in the war and nothing was left. So in 1996, I started work again. I had a large library, I had done a lot of research. I also did research on left-handed writers where I came up with some general rules. I also studied the signatures of alcoholics and drug addicts. They sometimes cause problems in banks when they try to -- when they try to get money from their accounts and so on. But this is all lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, can I take it that you didn't, did indeed not publish any more articles than the three mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I've explained that. I can explain again. I could have published 100 had there not been the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's enough, it's enough. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben, your next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, what is your definition of contentious documents? Are these referred to as questioned documents or contested documents, including signatures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, with reference to his report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. And in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. No, no. It's with reference to his report because it's in his report that he uses the terms contentious and non-contentious. He has explained already what he means, what he understands by non-contentious. Now he needs to explain what he means by contentious.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents which, at the request of the Defence team, were labelled as such. It was not I who labelled them as contentious. In other words, these were suspect documents. Whether they are contentious or not, that is for the Court to decide, Mr. Wubben. That's my response to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Professor, for the Defence to label?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the label used by the Defence team. I used S-1, S-2, S-3, S-4, whereas you used P or Q. You have to label the documents you are investigating. I was given them as contentious documents and I was given a precise mandate, within which I worked. Perhaps they are not contentious in the view of the Chamber or in your view, but that is something that time will show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Professor Bilic, the same applies with non-contentious documents, in your view?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by the same? Contentious and non-contentious are not the same thing. Please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have understood his question. His question is, you've explained that the terminology, contentious, is not something that you created but it's what you were presented with by the Defence; two types of documents, one type is contentious, one type is none contentious. In other words, he's asking you, I think it's a superfluous question because he's already given you the answer. What Mr. Wubben is asking you is this applies also for non-contentious documents. In other words, you decided that they were non-contentious because you were told that these were non-contentious. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, for that question I think we have to separate whether we are talking about non-contentious of Naser Oric or Hamdija Fejzic because this witness did give a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can visit that on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully agree with you but I think -- or, if he prefers to answer it now that he's heard what you have to say, he can do that. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will give my response. Contentious documents are defined as such in the mandate received from the Defence team. The non-contentious documents were collected not only from the Defence team. The Defence team did provide some of these but I gathered others and we also looked for the people themselves and asked them to write something, because the greatest confirmation for me that something is non-contentious, if I see somebody writing it down. This is something I have to establish, only when I have established this can I approach my investigation. That is basic, when you are doing this sort of investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear enough as well. Any further questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, what do you mean by the statement of your last mandate, that there has to be proof of the fact that a -- non-contentious documents are produced by the writer concerned?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Proof that something is non-contentious, what do you mean? I have tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. Mr. Wubben, can we go straight to the transcript of Monday's sitting and read exactly what, according to you, he said within the context in which he said it? Because there may be previous question and answer that are relevant. So.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you give it to me, I'll read it out to him, Mr. Wubben, because I don't have the transcript here. It's -- you can read it yourself as well but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you give the reference to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The reference to the Defence is on Monday, 22 minutes after ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the date on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 15 hours, 22 minutes, 53 seconds. There is a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 22 minutes, 53 seconds. Yes, how does the question start?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The question starts with, "as I say" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Okay. Can I read out myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, it's fine with me. It's a lengthy question but more lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why, this is what I suspected, that the answer may have been given in a particular context and I would rather prefer to put to the witness the entire context. There was this question put to you on Monday, Professor Bilic: That's, of course, Mr. Jones asking you. "As I say we are going to come to your report in detail in a moment but I still have one or two general questions. In referring to samples, you have referred to the importance of the quantity and quality of the samples. Now quantity, I imagine is self-explanatory; you need sufficient number of documents to analyse. But for quality can you explain a little bit what factors are relevant to the quality of the sample to be analysed?" And this is your answer: "I will give you a direct answer. The non-contentious document has to have sufficient quantities, of course, that's first. As for the quality, it has to do with the following categories. The way the non-contentious documents came into being. They must have come into being outside of the contentious documents. However, they should have come into being in that same year or the same month. But the year is sufficient. Secondly, they should be in their original form rather than photocopies. They should contain writings which were made in the same writing implements as the non-contentious, as the non-contentious documents. That's to say in ballpoint pen or in pencil and so on and so forth. Furthermore, there has to be proof of the fact that the non-contentious document was in fact produced by the writer concerned. How can we prove this? Well, this can be proved in the case of official documents, for instance. The quality of the documents has to be satisfactory. They have to be made on paper, which is of more or less the same quality, and so on and so forth. This is, I believe, enough. Everybody understands what I am saying." You were wrong. Mr. Wubben didn't. He wants an explanation now. This is the context and I think I was right in trying to put it in the context. You are now asked by Mr. Wubben to explain exactly what you mean to say when you say that there has to be proof of the fact that the non-contentious document was in fact produced by the writer concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand now and I will respond. The document has to form part of an official correspondence. The document signed by a person has to be a document sup as a pass port or an identity card or a document applying to open a bank account or something of that nature. So these are documents where the identity of the person has been checked. The official asking for the signature asks for an identity card or a passport and then the person who signs is given a form to sign. This is a signature which certainly belongs to the person, the writer. This document has nothing whatever to do with the contentious documents. Its purpose is to prove identity. Also, for example, there are documents people sign when getting money from their bank account or signing a cheque, for example, or a letter. Also, there are documents containing other proof that they were signed by the person concerned. For example, if they have an official stamp. If you look at my passport, for example, when I was entering the country here, they looked at my passport, they looked at the stamp, an at my signature and they looked at me. They didn't need any further proof of my identity. These are documents which exist in archives and are not generally available to one and all. There is a guarantee by an institution, a municipality, a ministry, a bank, which officially collected these signatures. Also, there are documents from private correspondence, for example, bills paid by the person, various kinds of receipts for the consignment of goods, for example, and there is a whole art in finding such documents. Once you have found such documents, you have signatures you can use without any problems. So there must be an uncontested sample of good quality and quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that answer your question, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: To a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uncontested means that there is a check of that signature by others than the originator himself or herself?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A check by others but also checked by me because ultimately I will look at each and every signature and I will look at the material critically. Before any investigation is undertaken, you have to look at the material critically, both a contentious and non-contentious material. Once we have collected these documents, if the person is still alive, the writer, we find the writer and ask them for their signature. That is how you create the material you use. This is fundamental for the investigation, because once you have samples of signatures, provided by the writer or the person to whom the signature belongs, then we can proceed without any problems. I hope I've been sufficiently precise now. I am familiar with my field and you are with yours, so I would find it easier to communicate with a colleague in my own field. I'm trying to simplify things as far as I can. I'm not sure I always manage to provide the kind of answer you require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We needn't bother about it any further because that's not going to stop Mr. Wubben from proceeding with his questions to you. So Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is relevant that someone is witnessing the placing of the signature?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, I refer now to one of the persons in your report, Mr. Hamdija Fejzic. You know Mr. Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to meet Mr. Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hamdija Fejzic present to you his so-called non-contentious documents mentioned in page 4 and 5, and paragraph [inaudible] of your report?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he came to see me in my laboratory, which is an official laboratory, well known in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he had to bring his identity card so I could establish his identity. On our identity cards, there is a photograph and a signature, which has been scanned. Once I established this, Mr. Fejzic spoke to me briefly. I explained to him that I had been recruited by the Defence team and that they had arranged this appointment and that's how things were. I then asked Mr. Fejzic to bring any official documents he had with him, the kind of documents I have described. He had other documents he couldn't give me, but he gave me two bank cards of Raiffeisen bank, which I compared with his identity card so I could be sure they were by the same person, Hamdija Fejzic, of his own free will, without any duress of coercion, gave me a sample of his handwriting and habitual signature. Once he had done this I thanked him. I told him I would return to him the official documents he had provided me with. They were official documents with his signature and the appropriate stamps. He didn't know anything else. He spontaneously wrote his signature several times on squared paper, which is how the sample was created. So I got to know Mr. Hamdija Fejzic when I saw him pursuant to the plan date given to me by the Defence team. That's my response with regard to Mr. Fejzic. Maybe I've spoken at too much length.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, with all respect indeed, it was a quite extensive answer and in the following questions, I will be -- yes, I will be forced to stop you because the only question was on the issue, do you know Mr. Hamdija Fejzic and, well, thank you for the information and I will now ask my specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because it's true that he had a lengthy -- but I think it was very useful, and your question was, did Mr. Hamdija Fejzic present to you his so-called non-contentious documents mentioned about -- so he answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I would like to know is this from the witness: It seems to me that you had at this time during your meeting with Hamdija Fejzic, two kinds of documents from him. One was documents that he brought with him, that he handed to you, and which you returned back to him, the so-called official documents with stamps, as you call them. The other documents that he signed there and then in your presence, specimens of his habitual handwriting and specimens of his handwriting. Did you keep those or did you give them back to Mr. Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for observing this, Your Honour. I kept these documents and handed them to the Defence, on condition that I told Mr. Fejzic that when these proceedings are over, the documents would be returned to him. He needs them in his archives. He doesn't need them urgently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor Bilic, in your report, you refer to five documents from Hamdija Fejzic. Apart from those five documents, can I take it that you received more samples of his signature, as you refer to receiving several samples from his signature in your laboratory?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, on page 4, under item 3, I exhaustively listed whatever samples I had. I do not wish to read them out here but everybody can see there is point N-1, N-2, N-3, N-4, and N-5, which can be found on page 5, and that's as I said one sheet of squared A4 paper which contains a sample of Hamdija Fejzic's handwriting and signatures taken on the 10th of November 2005. This was a good sample of Fejzic's signature, both in terms of quantity and quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Bilic, you stated that he placed in your presence several samples of his signatures. Is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are these samples in that list of N-1 up to N-5, Professor?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just answered that, Mr. Wubben, if you've been following me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the list of documents, only N-5 referred to the 10th of November 2005, and that's only one signature. Where are the other several samples or am I mistaken? Please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think will let him explain. Yes, Professor Bilic. If there is a problem we can go through these, N-1 to N-5 straight away. One by one and he will -- I think it's better. One moment. Okay. Finish with your answer first and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll give you my answer. Let us go back to page 4. Item 3, N.1., bank cards by Raiffeisen bank, DD, BiH Sarajevo. These were two bank cards, and each contains Hamdija Fejzic's signature. Furthermore, a receipt number such and such from Tuzla also containing Hamdija Fejzic's signature. In 3 on page 4, a sales contract, officially certified in the municipality, otherwise it wouldn't have been valid, number such and such, with the municipal court of Visoko which is a town near Sarajevo. N.4., preliminary contract on joint venture, also certified, with the municipal court one Sarajevo. This document is also certified. Therefore it must have been beyond doubt verified. That's to say the signature. And then N.4., one sheet of squared A4 paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there. Let's deal with these four documents or N.1., N.2., N.3., and N.4., right? Where are these documents now? This is what Mr. Wubben actually has asked you. Where are they now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that these documents were handed over to the Defence together with my findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Defence to the Defence or to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would wish them to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were they handed to the Defence or to Mr. Fejzic, these four documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that these documents were taken from me -- him to be kept until such time as the -- this procedure is over. These documents are here in their original form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to stop. I'm not going to ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, we apologise but it seems that the confusion has been caused by the translation of a word under N.5. It says one sheet of squared paper, in brackets it says, "handwriting and signatures by Hamdija Fejzic," whereas in the translation, it says signature. And expert Bilic was talking of signatures, in plural. And I believe that's the -- what caused the entire confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have two versions of testimony now which I want to clarify. Let's start with page 4 of your report, Professor Bilic. N.1., N.1., Raiffeisen bank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is that document, did you give it to Fejzic or to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to give the bank cards over to the man because he needed them. I have the photocopies. I examined the originals, of course, but I had to give him his cards back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have to go through them one by one. N.2., receipt number 14/2001, released in Tuzla, 24 April 2004, signed by Hamdija Fejzic. This N.2., did you give it back to Hamdija Fejzic or did you give it to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave that to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. N.3., sales contract verified copy of the 23rd September, did you give this to the Defence or to Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave that to the Defence and I said so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: N.4., preliminary contract.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same as above. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And N.5., containing handwriting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same as above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear. Last question. Last question is, apart from these N-1, N.2., N.3., N.4., and N.5., did you have any other documents which were made available to you by Hamdija Fejzic or by the Defence, for examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was quite sufficient and there was no need for me to seek anything further. Had it been necessary I could have sought more but it hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To make sure that the various signatures that Hamdija Fejzic signed in your presence, and the specimen handwriting, were all in this one checked A4 sheet and not on several pieces of paper? A4 it says here. N.5., in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: With respect, Your Honour has clarified the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said one sheet of paper, one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Just to put the final cross on the T, N.1. was a photocopy. He didn't actually say whether he provided that to the Defence or not. Other than that, Your Honour lass covered anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said that N.1. he gave back to the me ... MR. DI FAZIO: And he said he made a photocopy but I didn't say whether or not he provided the photocopy to the Defence, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of N.1. you made a photocopy of the credit card. What -- did you keep that photocopy yourself or did you hand that to the Defence? This is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to give it to the Defence. They had to see what the basis of my work was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have cleared this and I think Professor Bilic has been in the witness box for too long. I think we'll have a 30-minute break straight away. Everyone is getting tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I updated myself with a view to the two motions and extent of work they're needed for. It will be substantial even given the accent on -- only on the translations with a view to the motion P84, we are working on that from yesterday, we definitely need time into the coming week. The motion regarding the interview, Your Honours, that's not a matter so much for translation as for learning what the audio tapes itself reveal. It means a time-consuming listening to all the audiotapes mentioned, I'm updating what the outcome is and the outcome is that indeed we need substantial time for that, as we cannot do it ourselves, and need to rely on expertise in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you had a whole year and a half to do that. You've been put on notice all the time that the interpretation or the transcript was not correct. I'm not saying that it wasn't. I'm just saying that you were put on notice by the Defence that it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that's why -- and that's why, Your Honour, we kept up a correspondence with the Defence, even in November in that respect, and they refused to cooperate and to give to us their findings. Also, Your Honours, with a view to the interview, the Naser Oric interviews, there had already been an exercise of going through the interviews and that was more than a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway. Stop, please, Mr. Jones. Later on, during this sitting we are coming down with an order, oral order, giving you a time limit, both for the filing of the responses and even in relation to the rebuttal. So we've discuss it, we've come to a conclusion. I just want to itemise it one after the other, and my Senior Legal Officer is working on it. So that's the end of the discussion. Yes, further questions you might have for Professor Bilic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You must understand both of you that we need to finish this case. We simply cannot allow you to reopen almost the entire case at this point in time. It's unheard of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a question, a following question, related, Professor Bilic, to the document mentioned as N.5 on page 5 of your report. N.5 is -- and the Presiding Judge already referred to it is a checked A4 sheet a letter of 10 November 2005. Sarajevo handwriting and signatures. I appreciate the additional information by Defence counsel, signatures by Hamdija Fejzic. Now my question is, Professor Bilic, how many signatures did Hamdija Fejzic provide to you on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have that sheet of paper, please, to see how many signatures there are? I did not count them but there are many of them, quite a sufficient number. I would have to count them and if you have the document I would please like to have it. Or else, if you have the document before you, perhaps you can furnish us the number. If the Defence, that is, could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is the Defence counsel able to provide this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a surreptitious way of achieving the result that we end up tendering or offering precisely the documents which are in question. As we indicated before, we still have to revert as to whether we intend to disclose those documents at all and we are not in a position to make them available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your next question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your -- do you recall how many signatures, not the exact number, what was the number more than two or three or more than ten signatures? Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, there were quite a few of them, not one but several. I cannot recall at this time but the number was sufficient for an expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You provided, Professor Bilic, a bibliography of books and articles included in your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that one of the reports you referred to is the book called, "The Scientific Examination of Documents" by David Ellen?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the book I think very highly of. I translated it after having received it in 1999, I believe. It's a very good book and I can -- well, I could go through all of these but I would definitely not put on paper here any of the books that I did not read. I even have it in my room, if you want to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did include, Professor, this in your book -- in your bibliography because you regard his book as a solid and reliable text and handwriting and analysis, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only of handwriting but there are other relevant examinations of documents, and the author is a very experienced examiner. It's a very good book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to quote a part of this book, Professor Bilic. It's page 73 of that book, and I will ask the usher to provide copies of it, page 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could actually have the book? And as we all know, all of this matter is in context and rather than just one page. I don't know if that's actually going to be of assistance to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I would rather have the witness tell us himself. It's not one page. It's a whole -- what seems to be a whole chapter here, chapter 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's only page 73 that I will in this stage refer to. I have further questions but at this stage, I will only refer to one particular page and I don't think I need to provide the whole book in that respect, just a photocopy of the part of it and the initial page. Shall I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wonder whether the witness -- the expert witness has received it in the Bosnian language? We have not received it in the Bosnian language. That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it was written in the Bosnian language or published in the Bosnian language. I would be very surprised and I would think --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am aware of this. However, we always provide expert witnesses with translations in order for the witness to understand the text in his own language rather than hearing what Mr. Wubben is reading out aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do it in a different manner. Do you understand English? Do you read English and understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand very little, but I have a very good translator in Sarajevo who I go a long way back with and who provided me with a translation of the text. Your Honours, am I here to be tested in the field of graphology? And I am presented with different books here. Perhaps I should ask the Prosecutor about some of the books I have been using.
