I mentioned here only some segments of the book. I believe I am -- I should not be asked about one author only, about this particular author, David Ellen. There are other authors in the world that one can consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that to us, Professor Bilic, but, please, let us decide exactly which questions are to be allowed and which not. So, Mr. Wubben, I suggest that this is also made available to the interpreters. I can't see -- yeah, they have it. You have it as well. Yes, I see that they have it. You need to tell the interpreters in particular which part you're going to refer to, and this will be interpreted as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me first submit that this is not a choice by myself. This is a part of his bibliography he referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I have not entered into the question of whether you should put the question or not. Please proceed. And then we see afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to quote a part of page number 73, and it relates to signatures in bold. I start, "Signatures are important as known writings written in the course of business. A wide variety of these written without the knowledge that they may be later used as comparison material gives a better indication of the whole range of variation used by the writer than a small sample taken at one sitting. The documents listed above will provide useful sources for signatures, which can also be found on questionnaires, charge sheets, labels on exhibits, credit cards, and driving licences." Now, my question, Professor Bilic, first, is could you follow the quotation?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent I've understood it. Not the entire text but some of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, then we need to have it read out to him, translated again. I'll read it out slowly and the interpreters please try to interpret the text in the witness's language. "Signatures are important as known writings written in the course of business. A wide variety of these written without the knowledge that they may be later used as comparison material gives a better indication of the whole range of variation used by the writer than a small sample taken at one sitting. The documents listed above will provide useful sources for signatures, which can also be found on questionnaires, charge sheets, labels on exhibits, credit cards, and driving licences." All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now I'm waiting for the question that Mr. Wubben will put to me, but I understand it far better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Professor Bilic, you agree with the proposition from that book that whenever you request a sample, it's important that the sample of a signature is written without the knowledge that it may be later used as comparison material? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answers, I indicated that, and I absolutely agree with that, and thank God that we can get hold of such material, otherwise we would not be able to have conclusive findings on handwriting examination and we would not be able to pin down criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, when Hamdija Fejzic visited your laboratory, he did put samples of signatures on a sheet, didn't he? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your request, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before that, he gave me all the documents that he had brought along and I first checked his identity against an identity card that he gave me, and then we proceeded to the taking of the samples of handwriting and signatures, which he did of his own free will. It has to be subject to one's free will before one proceeds to taking a sample.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Professor Bilic, did Hamdija Fejzic put those signatures on that sheet knowing that he put these on that sheet in the field of an examination of handwritings and signatures?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he did it of his own free will, and in his own hand, and I told him before that that the sample was required for the document examination. I did not show him the contentious documents I had received from the Tribunal because I had received it along with an instruction that these ought not to be shown to the members of the public. I abided by the instructions, and he provided me with a sample of his own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now is the request to him by you in your laboratory to put samples of the signatures in the context of this handwriting examination and signature examination, contrary to the proposition in the book we just quoted?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his book, Mr. Ellen addresses only one part of the process of taking handwriting samples. In another part, he also showed -- talks about how the samples are to be taken. He is discussing this approach because he's talking about a -- signature samples that are to be taken this way. He put it rightly in saying that this was the best way of approaching examination, to have the documents written by the writer concerned, without his knowledge of the purpose of the writing. Therefore his signatures on the credit cards and so on and so forth as stated in this book. Therefore I don't see in what way this differs from what I did. I had Fejzic's credit cards, I had certain decisions and official documents, which were created independently of my examination, and then, in order to make the entire sample a better one, I asked Mr. Fejzic to give me a sample of his handwriting and a series of his signatures. I hope that I have been able to provide you with an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was Hamdija Fejzic who selected the signatures given to you under N.1 to N.4, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic brought with him quite a lot of documents, many documents that he had to keep and these documents which he was able to give me. So I took these and archived them for the purposes of the Defence and the Court. People need to keep their personal documents in their possession. They need to have them available. So you cannot take them. So it could not be otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had -- do I understand you correctly that you even received more documents than N.1 to N.4?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't kept them but you gave -- you returned them later on?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned them on the same day because these were documents that this person had to have. He could not relinquish them. I only took a look at them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't include it -- these other documents in your examination?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't, because I had to give them back to Mr. Fejzic. The Court can obtain these documents if need be but I had to give them back to him because he needed them. I could not deprive him of those documents. It was his labour permit and some other documents that he had to keep in his possession because he has his own company that he is in charge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did -- and did you photocopy those other documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did. I'm not able to remember at this point in time, but they were no longer relevant for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you choose to photocopy and to -- to photocopy documents and give the originals, to return the originals, because you considered the samples provided sufficient enough to do an examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered that question several times before, Mr. Wubben. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the thing. I think he's been extremely clear the documents were required by Hamdija Fejzic. He returned them. He may or may not have copied them and he included the ones in his answer which are in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the point needs to be elaborated any further, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you include the photocopies you made of those other documents as well in your examination?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not include any photocopies in my examination. I do not value photocopies. In my view, it would be useless. I would never include photocopies. The man was alive, he had brought sufficient quantities of documents and there was really no need to use photocopies and I would not use photocopies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I hate to interrupt you, but are you going to tender this extract from David Ellen's book into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. I ask for a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P617, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P617. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that whenever you are addressed with a photocopy, Professor Bilic, that you have no opinion?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means. I must have an opinion. But I cannot give a conclusive opinion. I always have certain reservations when dealing with photocopies, and I have explained this in my report on several pages. So, please, read that part of my report. I have told you what my general standpoint is with respect to photocopies, and Mr. Hilton and Mr. Ellen and all the others will tell you the same. The uses of photocopies are well known, and most experts would agree on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question: How can you, Professor Bilic, exclude any imitation or version within the alleged non-contentious documents? I mean, any imitations of versions from the originator, the alleged originator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to because otherwise this will elicit a very long answer. Let's separate the non-contentious documents into two parts, two kinds, two segments. The ones on which he himself witnessed handwriting and signature but we excluded, all right? So we are talking about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other non-contentious what have been classified as non-contentious documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the question is, Professor Bilic, the alleged non-contentious documents, N.1 up to N.4, how do you exclude the possibility of any imitations by the originator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Originator," again, needs to be explained but in this case, since we are talking of Hamdija Fejzic's document, do you mean originator being Hamdija Fejzic or someone else, because a credit card comes from a bank, a receipt comes from whoever issued it, and so on and so forth. What do you mean precisely by the originator?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it can be an imitation, imitation can be done by someone else than the one that is proposed to be the owner of the signature and can also be done with the person himself, Mr. Hamdija Fejzic, and then it's nor a pseudo imitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you back two days, Professor Bilic. Two days ago, in the very early stages of your testimony, you were asked to explain to us what you mean by non-contentious documents. And your answer was or the suggestion was, do you mean these documents you consider to be authentic? And your answer was yes. You considered these or you worked on the assumption that these were authentic documents. The question that is being put to you now by Mr. Wubben is the following: How sure can you be that what you considered to be authentic may, after all, not have been authentic at all? Would you give -- would you allow for that possibility? Would you allow for that possibility or not? We are talking of N.1, N.2, N.3, and N.4. Forget N.5 because N.5 was created in your presence. If I have not reflected the question rightly, please stop me and correct me, but I'm trying to make it a little bit more clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you at the outset that when Hamdija Fejzic arrived in my laboratory, the first thing he did was to show me his identity card because I don't know the man, I really don't know him. When I saw his identity card, it's a card showing his photographer and his scanned signature, and I've been doing this work for a long time. I took a look at this. After that we sat down. He had already brought documents with him. After that, I asked him to write his signature on squared paper because I wanted to observe his hand movements while he was writing, while at the same time observing the documents I had before me. I observed his hand movements, the way he formed the letters, how he positioned them on the piece of paper, the speed of writing. It would take a long time to describe everything. But I was convinced that these were his signatures. The signatures were on bank documents. You can have suspicions of documents, but there is such a thing as a re-test. That is why a sample has to be prepared and verified before one even begins to approach the expert investigation. There was not even a tiny microelement that gave rise to suspicion on my part or I would have investigated further and looked for more originals. I would have contacted the police, I would have looked at his passport. There are forms that he would have had to fill in and sign to obtain these documents. He would have had to deceive large numbers of people in order for me to be deceived also, and the possibility of that is extremely remote. It's very, very small. I think -- well, I've done my best to respond. The questions are rather broad and abstract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you satisfied with the answer, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then we can move to the next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one is why didn't you include that analysis, that examination, that observation, in your report?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't include it because this was simply preliminary. I focused on explaining my expert opinion. It would have been too voluminous to have included all this. Of course, I could have included it but it would have taken a fortnight to read the report then. I did not feel it necessary in view of my mandate but I did go through these preliminary stages because, I reiterate, that 90 per cent of the success of an expert investigation is proper preparation of the sample. I think I've been clear enough about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Professor Bilic. I think we need to cut down on the length of your answers. Please try to answer the -- any question as briefly as you can because otherwise you're going to be here Friday and even Monday, I'm trying to help you go back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish the truth to be established. I'm not in a hurry. I can testify for 10 days, if necessary. I don't want my testimony to be shortened and have things remain uncertain and obscure as a result. I want things to be done properly, as they should be, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben, your next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Related to the so-called non-contentious documents, with a view to Hamed Salihovic, how can you exclude any imitation or version within the alleged non-contentious documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to all of them, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because again they are not exactly all in the same category.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think to be practical, if there is one answer that you could give that would cover all the documents put together at one go, yes, go ahead. Otherwise I think it will be much more practical and quicker to go through this one document at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, can you give me one answer to that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. I'll do my best, Mr. Wubben. I understand your desire for me to explain everything and I will try. These are documents that could not be doubted. They were at Sarajevo university where the deceased Hamed Salihovic studied and obtained a degree in geography. As this man is deceased, everything had to be done and we could find a sample only at the university where he had studied. The rule is that these documents have to be archived for a hundred years. In his file, there were many samples of his handwriting in the period from 1969 to 1974. This was a continuous period of time. As such, it's true that there was a long time that elapsed between the creation of these documents and the expert investigation. But this was the only thing that could be done, the only sample that could be used. I have stated this with precision. All these documents are in the keeping of the Defence, so you can see them all, and everything I have listed here was collected by the Defence team and myself jointly. That's all I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One additional question. And on that basis you exclude the possibilities that there is in fact any imitation or version within those signatures and handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the professors who examined the deceased student were not so naive as to be taken in by imitations of his signature. He had to sign those documents himself. No one else could have done it for him. So I don't think there is any doubt here, that there was no disguise or imitation. Had I had any such suspicions I would not have taken this sample and used it in my analysis. I would have said that it would not be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Someone clarify this for me, please. In this category of documents, the Salihovic, N.8, N.9, N.10, N.11, and N.12, am I correct in saying that these have what is alleged to be a signature of the Accused as well on the face of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Knows are not. Which are the ones which have the signature of the Accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: These are in paragraph 2 subsequent on page 4, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Okay. I just wanted to make sure that -- all right. So basically, let's put it like this: From N.1 to N.12, these are all documents that were handed to you by the Defence, Professor Bilic. They are all -- they all referred to the period 1972, 1970 to 1974, the time when Salihovic was a student.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from 1969 to 1974, when he graduated. Yes, Your Honours. It took quite a long time to find this sample but we managed to find it in the end. It was my idea and this was all we could find where there could be no suspicion about the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the reasons are what you stated a few minutes ago, being university documents in the archives of the university. N.13, consisting in two --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- A4 sheet forms. Document by the Ministry of the Interior, CSB, Centre for Public Security Tuzla SJB, Srebrenica, number 18-13/09, 11118 of 1 August 1991, proposal for the nomination of the Skelani/Srebrenica unit commander, signature by Hamed Salihovic. On what basis do you exclude the possibility that this document may not be authentic, as far as the signature of Hamed Salihovic is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll respond. I listed the documents as given to me by the Defence. N.13 and N.14 are absolutely suspect. There was no way in which I could verify their authenticity, especially as we had no handwriting samples from the person himself, as he's not alive. That's why I had reservations about these two documents and I did not use them in my comparative analysis. I did use them in the photographic documentation but I, as an investigator did not trust those documents and that is my right as an expert. Let the Court decide about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor Bilic, for having made this clear. Yes, so you have got the entirety now, all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The documents in that category.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the category referred to Naser Oric, and listed, Professor Bilic, on page 4, under N.1 up to N.4, the so-called non-contentious documents. How truthful is it that Naser Oric is indeed the originator of the signature on the mentioned documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely truthful. First of all, for Naser Oric to be able to open his company, he had to go to the national audit service. This is the institution which issued permits for people to engage in enterprise -- in entrepreneurial activities. There were two forms he had to fill in and sign there, one for hard currency and another was a different form. He had to collect a lot of evidence in order to get the documents from this national audit service. This no longer exists. Now it's business banks who deal with such transactions. Therefore, there could be no doubt that those were his signatures. We also have the other documents that were in use in that company, containing his signature and a seal. We also had a number of signatures on the contentious documents, in the margin, on the 23rd of May 2001, or, rather, on the -- I took these into consideration and this was of specially importance. These were documents created between 1996 and 1999, at which time he had no idea that there would ever be an expert analysis of his signature on those documents. These were documents found in the national audit service and in the archives. For this reason, this was an absolutely sufficient sample. I don't wish to undervalue the other sample that was available to me, but this was very important. That's why there was no need for him to provide a sample again because there were these signatures already in existence written by him on the same day, and had there been any need, in 1993, for him to provide a sample, you could have obtained it from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need to have a very short break. I need to leave the courtroom for a while. --- Break taken at 5.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you. Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Professor Bilic, you explained referring to N.1 and N.5 up to N.12 for the source documents signed by Naser Oric, alleged signed -- to be signed by Naser Oric. And when it comes to N.2, N.3, and N.4, how did you exclude the possibility of imitations? How truthful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I need to clear this up. Who made these documents available, N.1, N.2, N.3, N.4, N.5? Who gave them to you? Or where did you get them from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got them from the Defence. The Defence knows where the documents come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that they are not in the record, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. And to confirm, Your Honour, N.5 up to N.12, those are the so-called known documents, K documents, K number 1 up to 8, under P100. N.5 to N.12, these are eight documents, so-called known signatures, provided by this Tribunal as P100. So my question focused on N.2 and N.3 and N.4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How truthful -- how could you indicate that these were the signatures from Mr. Naser Oric and no imitations or variations?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I compared these signatures with the signatures I had on the documents signed by Naser Oric on the 23rd of May 2001. I examined these signatures for the so-called matches, and I came to the conclusion that they were identical, consistently written, and that there was nothing that would give rise to suspicion about their truthfulness. I have included all these signatures into my photographic documentation. They are there to be seen and had there been any need I would have insisted that the Defence obtain from the Accused, Naser Oric, further samples of signature but there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me check something, Mr. Wubben, before you proceed. These documents from N.1 to N.4, were they original documents or were they photocopies of -- they were original documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were originals, yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question especially with regard to N.1, file of deposited signatures with ZPP Tuzla of 12 July 1996 with two non-contentious signatures by NO. How would you be able to be in possession of these documents in their original? Because I suppose that the original would be with the ZPP in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the originals from the Defence, and probably the Defence obtained the documentation from the ZPP Tuzla against receipt for the purposes of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have a question for clarification. You just said in your testimony, "I examined these signatures for the so-called matches. I think the signatures which Naser Oric have given, has signed, on the 23rd of May 2001, examined these documents for the so-called matches and I came to the conclusion that they were identical, consistently written, and that there was nothing that could give rise to suspicion about their truthfulness." And now the sentence I would like to ask you, "I have included all these signatures into my photographic documentation." Is that -- but I think, if I count them, are we now talking about Naser or about Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naser, about Naser Oric, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: If I count these non-contentious signatures in your list, you had, I think 14 signatures altogether, if I count correctly, but in your report, I can only find seven signatures. Could you perhaps explain this difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I indicated that a rather large number of signatures is to be found on the samples N.5 to N.12, and these are signatures that are found on the contentious documents at the top right-hand corner. There are several of them but I placed them together. These are signatures N.5 and N.6 on page 30 and N.7 and N.8, then N.8, N.10. However, N.1 comes from the other document, from the file of signatures deposited with the ZPP Tuzla, and you can see that that's the document. It has a stamp there. N.11 is the signature written on request of, probably, an investigator in 2001. N.3 comes from the document which is the offer for transportation of goods from 1999 containing Oric's signature. Then N.1 which contains two non-contentious documents, as we said. Then N.12, which also belongs to the batch of documents I indicated earlier. I did not take photographs of all, but this -- these are documents that are contentious where Oric signed his name and put a date. Then we have N.2, which is the "AOR" company, that's Oric's company, which is actually an itemised list of a bills of lading for the shipment of goods. These are all signatures that I analysed one against the other, that took most of the time, and I came to the conclusion that all these signatures were written by the same writer. Had I not come to that conclusive finding I would have sought other samples of his signature. I believe that the sample that I had was highly appropriate for the type of examination I carried out. We could have obtained thousands of Naser Oric's signatures but I believe that the sample we had was enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is an important conclusion, an important finding that you did, that in your opinion you believed that these signatures, N.1 up to N.4, were the signatures from Naser Oric upon your analysis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you include that analysis and findings in your report?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where? Can you please point out?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be on one of the pages. I'll tell you in a moment. From page 15, including page 16, page 17, 18, which is followed by the so-called C comparative stage, the comparison starts from page 29 and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can follow that, but my question is: You agree that this is an important analysis and finding that you examined N.1 up to N.5 -- sorry, N.1 up to N.4 as being truthful signatures by Naser Oric as a finding and you compared those with N.5 to N.12, and I asked you where is that finding and examination clarified in your report?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This finding, which I arrived at during the preliminary stage, I did not believe it necessary to expound it here. This was part of my preliminary work, which was also done in relation to all the other samples, and it was after that that I carried out the examination. I believe that that was the mandate that I was assigned. It was in this preliminary stage that I removed any suspicion that there may have been in relation to the non-contentious samples. Had I found anything that would give rise to suspicion, I would have contacted the Defence immediately to tell them that there was something wrong with the non-contentious sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut down this to its proper proportions. It's true, from what I can see, that there is no categoric, explicit declaration by the expert in his report. I confirm that these are the authentic, this is the authentic signature of Naser Oric, but if you read on page 21, the entire paragraph 2, then you have the reasons why he must have concluded that. Basically that would amount to precisely the same thing. He is basically explaining why he considered these to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You observed it correctly. On page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise we would have had an explanation of why these signatures were not non-contentious or were not going to be taken into consideration by him. Anyway, let's move forward and please feel free to put any questions you like, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Bilic, of the existence of more non-contested material than documents N.5 to N.12, being signatures placed by Naser Oric on original documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. You were mentioning both contentious documents and original documents. Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You enlisted N.5 up to N.12 as source documents signed by Naser Oric, isn't it? Page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are these documents N.5 to N.12 in evidence? They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. When I received documentation from the Registry, I also received documents which had non-contentious signatures at the top. They were written in ballpoint pen on photocopied, contentious material. I was quite surprised by this. Who would have allowed entries to be made in hand on contentious documents? Therefore, Naser Oric placed his signature at the top right-hand corner, probably on someone's request, and I was not happy with this because this is not the sort of documentation you use in examination, because if you have contentious documents, and 12 of them, or rather from N.5 to N.12, more of them, and then you ask someone to place their signature on this, I don't like that. However, I was satisfied that authentic signatures were placed in blue ballpoint pen. There was the time and the date when the signature was placed, and without any doubt, Naser Oric did put his signature on these documents. Otherwise, one could have his doubts in relation to all and sundry. I kept for myself the fact that I was not happy with the way the signature was placed but that's all I have to say about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, were you aware that apart from these eight documents, there were also, in addition, here at the Tribunal, 27 similar documents available with the signature of Naser Oric, the original signature of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to know that. I had only the documents sent to me by the Defence and by the Registry. I can only talk about what I had and what I had I indicated in my paper. You can see clearly, and I can show you, which signatures I used, which signatures I took photographs of and used in my examination. I only had the documents that I received from the Tribunal's office in Sarajevo and the Defence. And I'm talking about non-contentious documents because the Defence did not have the contentious document. I received those from the Tribunal. And there is documentation to that effect which shows when I received the documents from the Tribunal and when I returned them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, have you asked the provider or the Defence for more documents, whether or not there are more documents available, more signatures by Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask for any more because there was no need for that. I felt that I had a sufficient sample. I wasn't worried about which documents these were or where they came from. I believed that the sample sufficed. I did not want to -- I wanted to approach the job I was doing seriously, not make a parody out of it. If you have any further questions for me, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, Professor Bilic. But wouldn't that make you more happy as an examiner to have more documents, 27 documents, you know, with the original signature of the Accused?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you when you say that. However, findings can be made with a lesser sample. I believed we had a sufficient sample, and I made my findings. If you need that or if there is need for that, if there are signatures I haven't seen, you give -- if you can give me enough time, I will make findings in relation to these other signatures you believe are non-contentious as well. I did not shrink from that. I can do that as well, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at me, Professor Bilic. A bigger sample, anyhow is better, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. I am looking at you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A bigger sample anyhow is better, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't have to be a rule. Conditionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have laboured the point sufficiently, Mr. Wubben. His answer is I would have asked for more had I considered or come to the conclusion that I did not have enough. That's his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that it doesn't have to be a rule, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move to your bibliography. You listed a book, "Scientific Examination of Documents" by Ordway Hilton, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, go ahead. I don't have the book here with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you enlisted it on your bibliography, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did it because you regard this book as well as a solid and reliable text on handwriting and analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For document examination in general. You should read the title of the book carefully. Scientific examination of documents, not handwriting. And, of course, we could discuss what a document is and how it can be examined. This is one of the first books I read even before the war. I lost it in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to ask the usher to provide the parties, the witness, the expert, with a part of this book, an excerpt. And I refer to page 300. Your Honours, shall I quote or, as you did it previous time, it is from the part of the sentence, "Amount of standard writing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 300, Your Honour. "Amount of standard writing" up until, let's say, ten lines from under, "Including additional specimens can greatly fortify the finding." It's on Sanction, Your Honour, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Until "additional specimens can greatly fortify the findings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: From "amount of standard writing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He's trying to make my earn my salary today. "Amount of --" do the interpreters have a copy of the text already? Yes. "Amount of standard writing." Now, if as I go along, anything is not clear or is not interpreted to your satisfaction, Professor Bilic, please stop me and we will go through it again. Or else, we will go through it and if you have any problems --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I'll start. "The amount" -- we are dealing with "amount of standard writing." "The importance of an adequate amount of writing has already been emphasised as the keystone of good writing standards. There is a common belief that a writer can be positively identified from only one or two of his signatures. Unfortunately, this is far from the truth. Normal writing variation alone generally makes this impossible. Only with a quantity of material, therefore, can all the writing characteristics of an individual and the variations that usually occur from specimen to specimen, be accurately determined. "That everyone does not sign his name or write any combination of words in exactly the same way twice is one of the more complicating elements of handwriting identification. This natural variation must be revealed by the known writing. Variation in writing is a personal factor -- it is not the same for each individual either in extent or nature. Besides, it can be influenced by the conditions under which the writing was done. Here is the reason that no hard and fast rule can be set for a minimum number of signatures or a minimum amount of general handwriting. "With many problems, 10 or 20 signatures should constitute an adequate sample, but there are a certain number of cases that may require 30, 40 or even more signatures in order to accurately reveal the writer's habits, ability, and range of variation. Actually, it is poor policy for the investigator to be satisfied with the bare minimum when just a few additional specimens can greatly fortify the findings." Do you wish us to read it again to you, Professor Bilic, or is that enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is quite enough, Your Honour. This is basic knowledge, elementary school knowledge, for persons to -- who are laymen in the area to learn something about it. I don't know what the purpose of this is. I mentioned my samples several times, both their quantity and quality. I said many things. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest you stop and wait for the question, because you haven't been asked a question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought you had put a question to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, do you agree with the proposition that everyone does not sign his name exactly the same way twice, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can confirm that to you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's important for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also the proposition that this natural variation must be revealed by the known writing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second proposition that ten or 20 signatures might be sufficient but that sometimes even more might be needed to reveal the writer's habit, ability and range of variation?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that it is poor policy to be satisfied with just the bare minimum when just a few additional specimens can fortify the findings?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you put your question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And linked to that, that it is poor policy to be satisfied with the bare minimum when just a few additional specimens can fortify the findings? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is really true, as written by this author. I read this some 20 years ago. As for the number, quantity is not equivalent to quality. What matters is whether it is relevant. Ten signatures can be sufficient if their origin is beyond dispute. A person might have to provide as many as a thousand signatures over days, and this all depends on the nature of the investigation. You can have quantity but the quality also matters. Quantity and quality always have to go together. We can have a hundred non-contentious signatures of insufficient quality. For example, if it is written on a certain date, in a certain form, that can have special weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, my question now is: Why didn't you ask for any additional samples regarding the number of documents provided by the Defence in relation to Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need. I had quite enough. Had there been any need, I would have asked for more. You can count the signatures yourself. There were quite enough. They covered a long time period so that, as an investigator, I found this sufficient. I could proceed to make my analysis and reach my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I draw your attention to the beginning of the third paragraph of -- from the extract that I read out to the witness. And it starts with the words "with many problems." So that's the key to assessing well what is being stated in that paragraph. Otherwise, what's contained in the last sentence of the previous paragraph, namely that there is no hard and fast rule for a minimum number of signatures or a minimum amount of general handwriting is the general -- is the principle that one has to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously as the problems arise, you need more and more signatures, and the wise thing to do is to get as many as you can, if there are problems or the bigger the problems are. But there is what is basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's more or less answered. He's told you, in my expert opinion, I had enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And he didn't ask for more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's his problem, not -- or his decision, not mine. But he's answered you. He's told you, "I didn't have the need or didn't feel the need for more."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, when you noticed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Allow me about two, three minutes because I need to communicate to both of you time limits that we are setting for responses and so on and so forth. Three minutes before -- we'll be finishing in 15 minutes' time. Sorry, in ten minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, when you noticed that Hamed Salihovic related N documents, so-called non-contentious documents, refers to the years 1973, 1974, didn't you consider your examination rather limited, to compare those documents from 20 years' difference in time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained, this is a long time period, but one forms one's handwriting by the end of secondary school. Perhaps the first year at university. After that it doesn't change much. I did say that this was a limiting factor, and I did say I could only reach my conclusions at the level of most probably, and I abide by that. I was unable to get any more samples. It was not possible to get any more. But this was sufficient for me to reach conclusions both as regards the handwriting and as regards the signatures. I have shown this precisely in the maps I provided. I had no doubts about this. As a rule, when the person is deceased, and nothing else can be found but an expert opinion needs to be given, this is not completely satisfactory, but I did mention this as a limiting factor. I think this is quite clear. So there is no need to discuss it any further, although I will, of course, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Professor Bilic, take a look at me. I have a question for you. Did you ask for more -- did you ask for more samples from the Defence related to Hamed Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But the Defence was unable to find any more. That's why I had reservations about the sample. Anything else that could be found was suspect because I was unable to check it or establish the origin through the institutions that issued the documents. I based my expert analysis on Hamed Salihovic's file which I had, and I leave the rest to Their Honours to evaluate. I cannot look for something that isn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two other documents from 1991, Professor Bilic, weren't you in addition limited in your examination upon noticing that a quantity of two signatures closer to the time of the questioned documents was, and I quote you, "barely satisfying"?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I said that I did not investigate these documents. I simply listed them because they were given to me by the Defence. But I did not consider them to be relevant because I was unable to verify their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do an examination to compare those two documents with the other N documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I discovered an absolute difference. The difference was truly astonishing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these documents, these two documents, makes a difference in your comparisons with the 20 years elder documents, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it tell you that about those two documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't reach any conclusions about those documents. As I said, I left them aside as suspect. That's why I could not use them in my comparison. I explained this. I listed them because I received them from the Defence but it was up to me to evaluate what was relevant and what I could use as relevant to my investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why -- what do you mean with the words, "barely satisfying"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After there question we need to stop, Mr. Wubben, so that I communicate to you the other matters. And then we continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question, Professor Bilic, is what do you mean with "barely satisfying" in this context?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I used the word "satisfying." What I said was that I could not accept them as authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you used that word, "satisfying," in your report, on page 20. Fourth line.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said quantitatively, although they are close to the time, in quality they are only conditionally satisfying. I didn't say barely. I said quantitatively there are only two of them, and they are only conditionally satisfying. I think this is quite precise. I did not use the word barely. I used the word conditionally. And then I went on to explain. You have surely read what I went on to explain. If you go on to look at the text, I underlined "conditionally" and then if you look at what it says further on, you will understand what I really wanted to present here to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, we need to stop here for today. We will continue tomorrow in the evening as well, in the afternoon. Yes, we need to give this document a number. This will become P618, 618. The Hilton, Ordway Hilton extract will become 618. Madam Usher, you can escort Professor Bilic. Have a nice evening, Professor Bilic, and we'll see you tomorrow. You still believe that you will be able to finish tomorrow, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: At the beginning of this session, I believed to be so but not at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It depends on the length of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So let's take these matters up. There are two motions from the Defence, one motion to exclude the alleged record of the Accused pursuant to Rule 89(D) and 95. That's the alleged interview. And a motion for revised translation of Prosecution exhibit P84. We have discussed amongst ourselves. We have decided to give you up to Tuesday, the 31st of January to file your responses to these two motions, Mr. Wubben. We are also giving you, Madam Vidovic, up to Tuesday, the 31st of January, time to file your response on the motion for rebuttal. Seven days. We are reducing it to seven days. You will then have two days from filing or from service of filing, obviously, to respond to the response, if you feel the need to do so. Then, within a very short period of time, one day, maximum, two days, expect our decision on rebuttal. Madam Vidovic, we would also require from you, if you intend to file a motion for rejoinder, to file same by Monday, the 6th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may address the Bench with respect to the last deadline, for our rejoinder by Monday, the 6th of February. Your Honours, if the decision is unfavourable to us, we will certainly ask for leave to appeal. So we ask that Your Honours bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, obviously, this is all taken consideration of, and also we might ultimately decide that there will not be rebuttal. So if there is no rebuttal, obviously there is not going to be a rejoinder. But let's take everything in its stride. If there is a motion for rejoinder, that means we need to have it by the 6th of February. If it is filed by the 6th of then, then you have two days, that's February the 2nd -- 8, February the 8th, to respond, Prosecution. If there is an acceptance for rebuttal, no appeal, then we plan to start the testimony of any rebuttal witnesses on February the 8th. On February the 10th, if there is -- if it's the case, we will decide on the rejoinder motion, and if that is the case, you are and will be expected to start with the rejoinder witnesses on the 14th of February. This is more or less what we have planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just make one observation, Your Honour, which is that as far as rebuttal is concerned, it's not simply a question of which witnesses the Prosecution will be allowed to call in rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at all, because obviously we haven't heard your objections and we haven't even started thinking in our mind about the individual ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. It's simply to say this, that even once you've rendered that decision, in fact it will also be a function of what the witnesses say in the -- in evidence. So subject to the fact that we might vary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure that that is all what we intend to do. When I say rejoinder by a certain date, obviously if the need for rejoinder arises out of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What's going on in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I don't need to given you any guarantees in writing because you know that that is so and will be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, that's is what we planned. You need to understand that at this point in time we cannot allow everyone to have the luxury of -- we ourselves cannot allow ourselves to have the luxury of as much time as we would like. I mean, we would like to have more time but I don't think we are in a position to allow that. So I thank everyone for your cooperation. We will continue tomorrow and make an effort to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
